newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan seals capital to block Islamist protest.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan seals capital to block Islamist protest.

text.p: Pakistani riot police threw a tight security cordon around the capital on Sunday to prevent Islamic radicals from holding a "million-strong" anti-corruption sit-in outside parliament.
"We've been ordered to foil this sit-in at all costs," said one of several hundred police in riot gear manning a barricade between Islamabad and its sister city of Rawalpindi.
"We've been on duty since four a.m. (2300 GMT Saturday) and we haven't let a single suspect person into Islamabad," he said.
Qazi Hussain Ahmad, leader of the opposition Jamaat-i-Islami (JI) party, denounced Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto's government for attributing violent intentions to his followers.
"The rulers have been considering the country their personal property," he said in a statement on Saturday. "Present state policies have made the life of common lot miserable."
He said JI had never been lawless and urged his supporters to show restraint. The government would be responsible for any "brutal use of force against peaceful protesters", he warned.
Police blocked access roads with barbed wire and containers hoisted into place by cranes. They set up sandbagged posts and deployed armoured vehicles and water cannons at key crossroads.
Cellular telephone services went dead on Saturday night, although there was no official confirmation that they had been deliberately cut off to disrupt JI communications.
Early in the morning there was no sign of the one million demonstrators the JI had planned to bring into Islamabad to join the sit-in outside the National Assembly (lower house) building.
Hundreds of police, some on horseback, stood by at Committee Chowk, a roundabout in central Rawalpindi, ready to turn back any JI activists trying to take the road to the capital.
That roadblock is near Liaquat Bagh, a large park where JI demonstrators were expected to gather ahead of their march.

The authorities had diverted or cancelled 24 passenger trains on Saturday, re-routing inter-city services to avoid Rawalpindi. Railway officials said reimbursing passengers would cost an estimated 15 million rupees ($373,000).
Earlier, paramilitary forces were drafted into the capital, replacing police who normally guard foreign missions.
In another sign of tension, Islamabad's International School, mainly for American and other foreign children, announced that it would stay closed on Sunday as a precaution.
JI leaders said the security forces had rounded up more than 5,500 of its supporters to try to disrupt the planned sit-in.
An Interior Ministry spokesman said the JI figure for detainees was exaggerated, but could not say how many people had been seized. He denied that the party's leader was being sought.
"All this fuss is a smokescreen designed to hide what they know will be a failed event," he said.
On Thursday Interior Minister Naseerullah Babar offered to release all JI detainees if the party agreed to shift the venue of its sit-in to a park in the nearby city of Rawalpindi.

JI rejected the offer as well as a suggestion by President Farooq Leghari that the sit-in be held in Islamabad, but not at parliament, which is close to the presidential palace, the prime minister's house, government offices and the diplomatic enclave.
Three people were killed and 60 wounded when gunfire broke out during a JI demonstration in Rawalpindi in June.
Some newspaper commentators criticised JI, which won only three seats in parliament at the last election in 1993, for courting more bloodshed by going ahead with its protest.

"Qazi (Hussain Ahmad) is aware of the dangers and by persisting with his sit-in plans is deliberately provoking a confrontation that will produce nothing but dead bodies," said a commentator in the English-language daily The News.
